claim: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) can be used to infer axonal connectivity because it is sensitive to axonal alignment, but it has limited spatial resolution and specificity.
source: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) can be used to infer axonal connectivity because it is sensitive to axonal alignment, but it has limited spatial resolution and specificity.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities and limitations of dMRI, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Scattered light imaging (SLI) and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) reveal axonal orientations with microscopic resolution and high specificity, respectively.
source: Scattered light imaging (SLI) and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) reveal axonal orientations with microscopic resolution and high specificity, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of SLI and SAXS, presented as established knowledge.

claim: SLI and SAXS quantitatively agree regarding in-plane fiber orientations including crossings.
source: SLI and SAXS quantitatively agree regarding in-plane fiber orientations including crossings, while dMRI agrees in the majority of voxels with small discrepancies.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data comparing the two methods.

claim: dMRI agrees with SLI and SAXS in the majority of voxels with small discrepancies.
source: SLI and SAXS quantitatively agree regarding in-plane fiber orientations including crossings, while dMRI agrees in the majority of voxels with small discrepancies.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data comparing dMRI to SLI and SAXS.

claim: SAXS and dMRI confirm theoretical predictions regarding SLI determination of through-plane fiber orientations.
source: We further use SAXS and dMRI to confirm theoretical predictions regarding SLI determination of through-plane fiber orientations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from SAXS and dMRI validating theoretical predictions.

claim: Scattered light and X-ray imaging can provide quantitative micrometer 3D fiber orientations with high resolution and specificity.
source: Scattered light and X-ray imaging can provide quantitative micrometer 3D fiber orientations with high resolution and specificity, facilitating detailed investigations of complex fiber architecture in the animal and human brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: With voxel sizes typically down to a few hundred micrometers in post-mortem human brains, the resolution of dMRI is insufficient to resolve individual nerve fibers.
source: However, with voxel sizes typically down to a few hundred micrometers in post-mortem human brains (Calabrese et al., 2018; Roebroeck et al., 2019), the resolution is insufficient to resolve individual nerve fibers, and isolating the anisotropic signal coming from myelinated axons alone is challenging.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge about dMRI limitations.

claim: Isolating the anisotropic signal coming from myelinated axons alone in dMRI is challenging.
source: However, with voxel sizes typically down to a few hundred micrometers in post-mortem human brains (Calabrese et al., 2018; Roebroeck et al., 2019), the resolution is insufficient to resolve individual nerve fibers, and isolating the anisotropic signal coming from myelinated axons alone is challenging.
evidence: This is a statement about a known limitation of dMRI, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Up to hundreds of fibers within a dMRI voxel might have complicated geometries, e.g., crossing or kissing fibers, which poses a challenge.
source: Moreover, up to hundreds of fibers within a voxel might have complicated geometries, e.g., crossing or kissing fibers, which poses a further challenge.
evidence: This is a statement about the complexity of fiber architecture within dMRI voxels, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) provides myelinated nerve fiber orientations by studying the anisotropy of myelin diffraction (Bragg) peaks in X-ray scattering patterns.
source: Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) provides myelinated nerve fiber orientations by studying the anisotropy of myelin diffraction (Bragg) peaks in X-ray scattering patterns (Figure 1A and C – Georgiadis et al., 2020; Georgiadis et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement describes the principle of SAXS and is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Myelin diffraction peaks in SAXS are generated by the interaction of the incoming X-ray photons with the layered structure of the myelin sheath.
source: These are generated by the interaction of the incoming X-ray photons with the layered structure of the myelin sheath, which surrounds nerve fibers in the white matter.
evidence: This is an explanation of the physical mechanism underlying SAXS, representing established knowledge.

claim: SAXS can be tomographic (SAXS tensor tomography).
source: The method can be tomographic (SAXS tensor tomography – Liebi et al., 2015; Schilling et al., 2019a; Georgiadis et al., 2021), and 3D-scanning SAXS (3D-sSAXS) can provide 3D distributions of axon orientations in tissue sections (Georgiadis et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating tomographic SAXS.

claim: 3D-scanning SAXS (3D-sSAXS) can provide 3D distributions of axon orientations in tissue sections.
source: The method can be tomographic (SAXS tensor tomography – Liebi et al., 2015; Schilling et al., 2019a; Georgiadis et al., 2021), and 3D-scanning SAXS (3D-sSAXS) can provide 3D distributions of axon orientations in tissue sections (Georgiadis et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work demonstrating 3D-sSAXS capabilities.

claim: SAXS can exploit the modulations in the azimuthal position of the myelin-specific Bragg peaks to resolve crossing nerve fiber populations across species with resolutions of tens of micrometers.
source: Recent studies further revealed that SAXS can exploit the modulations in the azimuthal position of the myelin-specific Bragg peaks to resolve crossing nerve fiber populations across species with resolutions of tens of micrometers (Georgiadis et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to recent work demonstrating this capability.

claim: The scattering of visible light can be used to reveal crossing nerve fiber orientations.
source: The scattering of visible light can also be used to reveal crossing nerve fiber orientations (Figure 1B – Menzel et al., 2020a; Menzel and Pereira, 2020b) as it is sensitive to directional arrangements of myelinated axons (~μm diameter).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Light scattering is sensitive to directional arrangements of myelinated axons (~μm diameter).
source: The scattering of visible light can also be used to reveal crossing nerve fiber orientations (Figure 1B – Menzel et al., 2020a; Menzel and Pereira, 2020b) as it is sensitive to directional arrangements of myelinated axons (~μm diameter).
evidence: This is a statement about the physical basis of light scattering in brain tissue, representing established knowledge.

claim: SLI has been shown to reliably reconstruct up to three in-plane fiber orientations for each image pixel with an accuracy of +/−2.4°.
source: SLI has been shown to reliably reconstruct up to three in-plane fiber orientations for each image pixel (with an accuracy of +/−2.4°; Menzel et al., 2021a) and an in-plane resolution at the micrometer scale (Menzel et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating SLI capabilities.

claim: SLI has an in-plane resolution at the micrometer scale.
source: SLI has been shown to reliably reconstruct up to three in-plane fiber orientations for each image pixel (with an accuracy of +/−2.4°; Menzel et al., 2021a) and an in-plane resolution at the micrometer scale (Menzel et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work demonstrating SLI resolution.

claim: A combined measurement of 3D-sSAXS and SLI can potentially provide a gold standard for imaging complex nerve fiber orientations in thin brain sections with micrometer resolution.
source: Hence, a combined measurement of 3D-sSAXS and SLI, with the high specificity to myelinated fibers of the former and the high-resolution capabilities of the latter, can potentially provide a gold standard for imaging complex nerve fiber orientations in thin brain sections with micrometer resolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complementary capabilities of the two methods, representing an inference.

claim: For in-plane nerve fibers, the strongest signal in both SLI and SAXS is perpendicular to the fiber orientation.
source: For in-plane nerve fibers, i.e., nerve fibers that mostly lie within the section plane, the strongest signal in both SLI and SAXS is perpendicular to the fiber orientation (red dashed lines in Figure 2B and C (i)), shown in the azimuthal profile as peaks lying 180° apart.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 2.

claim: For in-plane nerve fibers, the azimuthal profile shows peaks lying 180° apart.
source: For in-plane nerve fibers, i.e., nerve fibers that mostly lie within the section plane, the strongest signal in both SLI and SAXS is perpendicular to the fiber orientation (red dashed lines in Figure 2B and C (i)), shown in the azimuthal profile as peaks lying 180° apart.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 2.

claim: For two in-plane crossing fiber bundles, the peaks in the SLI and SAXS azimuthal profiles indicate the fiber orientations, with each bundle producing two peaks lying 180° apart.
source: For the two in-plane crossing fiber bundles in the corona radiata (ii), the peaks in the SLI and SAXS azimuthal profiles similarly indicate the fiber orientations, with each bundle producing two peaks lying 180° apart (white/yellow arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 2.

claim: For partly out-of-plane fibers, the peaks in the SAXS azimuthal profiles are still 180° apart but become less pronounced with increasing out-of-plane fiber angle.
source: For partly out-of-plane fibers, i.e., fibers that have a certain angle with respect to the section plane, such as those in the fornix, the peaks in the SAXS azimuthal profiles are still 180° apart - owing to the center-symmetry of the pattern -, but become less pronounced with increasing out-of-plane fiber angle (compare peak height of SAXS, Figure 2C (i) vs. (iii)).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 2.

claim: For partly out-of-plane fibers, the between-peak distance in the SLI azimuthal profiles decreases with increasing fiber inclination.
source: In contrast, the between-peak distance in the SLI azimuthal profiles decreases with increasing fiber inclination (SLI, Figure 2C (iii)), as also predicted by simulation studies (Menzel et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 2 and citations to simulation studies.

claim: For out-of-plane fibers that run almost perpendicular to the section plane, both the SLI scattering pattern and the SAXS myelin ring become almost radially symmetric without significant peaks in the azimuthal profile.
source: For out-of-plane fibers that run almost perpendicular to the section plane (Figure 2 point (iv), cingulum), both the SLI scattering pattern and the SAXS myelin ring become almost radially symmetric without significant peaks in the azimuthal profile.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 2.

claim: For fibers almost perpendicular to the section plane, the information about the in-plane fiber orientations is limited.
source: In such cases, the information about the in-plane fiber orientations is limited, whereas the out-of-plane angle can be retrieved with scans at different rotation angles using 3D-sSAXS (Georgiadis et al., 2020), and approximated in SLI (Menzel et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: The out-of-plane angle for fibers almost perpendicular to the section plane can be retrieved with scans at different rotation angles using 3D-sSAXS.
source: In such cases, the information about the in-plane fiber orientations is limited, whereas the out-of-plane angle can be retrieved with scans at different rotation angles using 3D-sSAXS (Georgiadis et al., 2020), and approximated in SLI (Menzel et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The out-of-plane angle for fibers almost perpendicular to the section plane can be approximated in SLI.
source: In such cases, the information about the in-plane fiber orientations is limited, whereas the out-of-plane angle can be retrieved with scans at different rotation angles using 3D-sSAXS (Georgiadis et al., 2020), and approximated in SLI (Menzel et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The in-plane nerve fiber orientations from SAXS and SLI are highly coincident, not only for unidirectional fibers, but also for fiber crossings.
source: The in-plane nerve fiber orientations are highly coincident, not only for unidirectional fibers, but also for fiber crossings, depicted as colored lines in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, where each vector glyph covers orientations from a grid of 165 × 165 measured pixels that are visually overlaid in SLI, vs. a 5 × 5 pixel grid in SAXS.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 3.

claim: In the corona radiata, the fibers of the corpus callosum fan out while crossing the ascending internal/external capsule.
source: Further zooming in shows a concordant fiber course in the highly complex corona radiata architecture (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E): the fibers of the corpus callosum fan out (blue/magenta) while crossing the ascending internal/external capsule (green).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 3.

claim: For regions with one fiber orientation in the vervet brain, the mean angular difference between SLI and SAXS is ~0.017° and the median absolute difference is ~4.1°.
source: The two histograms show a distribution around zero degrees (one fiber orientation: mean ~0.017°, median absolute ~4.1°; two fiber orientations: mean ~0.316°, median absolute ~5.6°).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 4.

claim: For regions with two fiber orientations in the vervet brain, the mean angular difference between SLI and SAXS is ~0.316° and the median absolute difference is ~5.6°.
source: The two histograms show a distribution around zero degrees (one fiber orientation: mean ~0.017°, median absolute ~4.1°; two fiber orientations: mean ~0.316°, median absolute ~5.6°).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 4.

claim: The main fiber orientations per pixel for dMRI and 3D-sSAXS show a high correlation, with a dot product approximating unity.
source: The main fiber orientations per pixel for dMRI and 3D-sSAXS (Figure 5C) show a high correlation, similar to what has been shown in Georgiadis et al., 2020, with a dot product approximating unity (Figure 5E), and a median angular difference of 14.4o over all voxels (9.1o over voxels with fractional anisotropy (FA) >0.2, computed from the eigenvalues of the rank-2 tensor for both methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 5 and a citation.

claim: The median angular difference between dMRI and 3D-sSAXS main fiber orientations is 14.4° over all voxels.
source: The main fiber orientations per pixel for dMRI and 3D-sSAXS (Figure 5C) show a high correlation, similar to what has been shown in Georgiadis et al., 2020, with a dot product approximating unity (Figure 5E), and a median angular difference of 14.4o over all voxels (9.1o over voxels with fractional anisotropy (FA) >0.2, computed from the eigenvalues of the rank-2 tensor for both methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 5.

claim: The median angular difference between dMRI and 3D-sSAXS main fiber orientations is 9.1° over voxels with fractional anisotropy (FA) >0.2.
source: The main fiber orientations per pixel for dMRI and 3D-sSAXS (Figure 5C) show a high correlation, similar to what has been shown in Georgiadis et al., 2020, with a dot product approximating unity (Figure 5E), and a median angular difference of 14.4o over all voxels (9.1o over voxels with fractional anisotropy (FA) >0.2, computed from the eigenvalues of the rank-2 tensor for both methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 5.

claim: In the corona radiata, the two methods (dMRI and SAXS) have a median angular difference of 5.6° in the first orientation, and 6.0° in the second orientation.
source: First, in the challenging region of the corona radiata, where multiple fiber crossings occur, the dMRI fiber orientations seem to be in high agreement with the direct structural X-ray scattering (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B left): the two methods have a median angular difference of 5.6o in the first orientation, and 6.0o in the second orientation (overall median angular difference 5.8o).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 5.

claim: Diffusion MRI has the sensitivity to accurately resolve multiple fiber orientations per voxel in the white matter.
source: This shows that diffusion MRI has the sensitivity to accurately resolve multiple fiber orientations per voxel in the white matter, see also Figure 5D and F (rectangle i, orange in the corona radiata).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, supported by Figure 5.

claim: In the corpus callosum, the main fiber orientations from dMRI and SAXS were in high agreement, with a median angular difference of 5.7°.
source: Next, we turned our focus to areas that appear to have relatively homogeneous fiber populations in SAXS, such as the corpus callosum. The main fiber orientations in these regions were again in high agreement between the two methods, with a median angular difference of 5.7o (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B, right).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Unlike X-ray scattering, which shows homogeneous fiber orientations in the corpus callosum, dMRI seems to show multiple fiber orientations per voxel, with a secondary fiber population perpendicular to the main one.
source: There was an observed difference in detecting secondary orientations in areas such as the corpus callosum. Unlike X-ray scattering, which shows homogeneous fiber orientations, dMRI seems to show multiple fiber orientations per voxel, with a secondary fiber population perpendicular to the main one (albeit with a much smaller magnitude).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data comparing dMRI and SAXS.

claim: SLI confirms the X-ray scattering results and does not observe a second fiber population perpendicular to the main one in the corpus callosum.
source: Referencing these regions in the micrometer-resolution SLI (px = 3 μm, Figure 5H), we confirm the X-ray scattering results and do not observe a second fiber population perpendicular to the main one.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 5H.

claim: Comparing the SAXS and dMRI secondary orientations in the posterior brain section, there was a 104% increase in the voxels with multiple orientations in dMRI.
source: We then proceeded to quantify this effect over the entire white matter of the posterior brain section. Comparing the SAXS and dMRI secondary orientations, we observed a 104% (more than double) increase in the voxels with multiple orientations in dMRI.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: Secondary fiber orientations within a single voxel were detected in 31% of the total number of voxels by SAXS vs. 64% of the total number of voxels by dMRI in the posterior brain section.
source: More specifically, secondary fiber orientations within a single voxel were detected in 31% of the total number of voxels by SAXS vs. 64% of the total number of voxels by dMRI (also see Figure 5—figure supplement 5 for a map of the number of orientations per voxel).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The anterior brain section showed a 40% increase in voxels with multiple orientations in dMRI compared to SAXS.
source: The anterior brain section similarly showed a 40% increase, while primary orientations were in high agreement as well (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Theory suggests that the fiber inclination is directly related to the distance between the two peaks in the SLI azimuthal profile.
source: Theory suggests that the fiber inclination is directly related to the distance between the two peaks in the SLI azimuthal profile (upper Figure 2C).
evidence: This statement refers to theoretical predictions, supported by reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The peak distance in SLI should decrease with increasing inclination.
source: The peak distance should decrease with increasing inclination, as indicated by the black dashed curves in Figure 6G, which were computed from simulated SLI azimuthal profiles for fiber bundles with different inclinations (Menzel et al., 2021a, Figure 7d).
evidence: This statement refers to theoretical predictions from simulations, supported by citation and Figure 6G.

claim: The out-of-plane inclination angles from dMRI highly agree with those obtained from 3D-sSAXS.
source: The out-of-plane inclination angles from dMRI (Figure 6C) highly agree with those obtained from 3D-sSAXS (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 6.

claim: In both coronal brain sections (vervet and human), the fibers in the corpus callosum are mostly oriented in-plane (α<20°).
source: In both coronal brain sections (vervet and human), the fibers in the corpus callosum (cc) are mostly oriented in-plane (dark blue: α<20°), while fibers in the cingulum (cg) are mostly oriented out-of-plane (light green/yellow: α>40°).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 6.

claim: In both coronal brain sections (vervet and human), fibers in the cingulum are mostly oriented out-of-plane (α>40°).
source: In both coronal brain sections (vervet and human), the fibers in the corpus callosum (cc) are mostly oriented in-plane (dark blue: α<20°), while fibers in the cingulum (cg) are mostly oriented out-of-plane (light green/yellow: α>40°).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 6.

claim: Fibers in the vervet fornix show mostly intermediate inclination angles (20°<α<40°).
source: Fibers in the vervet fornix (Figure 6A) show mostly intermediate inclination angles (light blue: 20°<α<40°).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: Regions with in-plane fibers (corpus callosum) contain many image pixels with large peak distances (Δ>170°) in SLI.
source: When comparing the inclination angles to the corresponding SLI peak distances in Figure 6D–E (evaluated for regions with a single detected fiber orientation), it becomes apparent that regions with in-plane fibers (cc) contain many image pixels with large peak distances (blue: Δ>170°), whereas regions with out-of-plane fibers (cg) contain many image pixels with notably smaller peak distances (green/yellow: Δ<140°) – especially in the human cingulum.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 6.

claim: Regions with out-of-plane fibers (cingulum) contain many image pixels with notably smaller peak distances (Δ<140°) in SLI.
source: When comparing the inclination angles to the corresponding SLI peak distances in Figure 6D–E (evaluated for regions with a single detected fiber orientation), it becomes apparent that regions with in-plane fibers (cc) contain many image pixels with large peak distances (blue: Δ>170°), whereas regions with out-of-plane fibers (cg) contain many image pixels with notably smaller peak distances (green/yellow: Δ<140°) – especially in the human cingulum.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 6.

claim: The scatter plots confirm a decreasing peak distance with increasing fiber inclination for most regions.
source: The scatter plots confirm a decreasing peak distance with increasing fiber inclination for most regions, matching the prediction by simulations.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 6G.

claim: The broadly distributed points from the cingulum might be due to the fact that the peak distance in regions with highly inclined fibers is harder to determine due to less pronounced peaks.
source: The broadly distributed points from the cingulum might be due to the fact that the peak distance in regions with highly inclined fibers is harder to determine due to less pronounced peaks (Figure 2C (iv)).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing an inference.

claim: The cingulate gyrus is interspersed with a transverse rather in-plane fiber bundle, which explains the large SLI peak distances in some regions of the white matter cingulate gyrus.
source: The dMRI orientation distribution functions (Figure 6F) reveal indeed that – in addition to the cingulum bundle with highly inclined fibers (in green) – the cingulate gyrus is interspersed with a transverse rather in-plane fiber bundle (in red), which explains the large SLI peak distances in some regions of the white matter cingulate gyrus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, supported by Figure 6F.

claim: SAXS and SLI highly agree in areas of both single and crossing fiber orientations.
source: SAXS and SLI highly agree in areas of both single and crossing fiber orientations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: SLI provides information about 3D-fiber orientations.
source: Taking the main out-of-plane fiber orientations from dMRI and SAXS into account, we could show that SLI provides information about 3D-fiber orientations, but is still limited in the quantification of the out-of-plane angles, especially in regions with crossing fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: SLI is still limited in the quantification of the out-of-plane angles, especially in regions with crossing fibers.
source: Taking the main out-of-plane fiber orientations from dMRI and SAXS into account, we could show that SLI provides information about 3D-fiber orientations, but is still limited in the quantification of the out-of-plane angles, especially in regions with crossing fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The combined SAXS and SLI measurements show that both methods can provide a reliable reference for axonal orientation maps.
source: The combined SAXS and SLI measurements, with the unbiased resolving power of SAXS and the high-resolution power of SLI show that both methods can provide a reliable reference for axonal orientation maps, towards a gold standard to which other techniques such as dMRI can be compared.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and cross-validation.

claim: Histological staining has limitations in white matter regions with densely packed nerve fibers.
source: Histological staining allows to study nerve fiber organizations with fine structural detail (Amunts et al., 2013; Carriel et al., 2017), but has limitations in white matter regions with densely packed nerve fibers.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of histological staining, supported by citations and representing established knowledge.

claim: Structure-tensor analysis of Nissl-stained histology slides can reveal glial cell orientation along axons.
source: Structure-tensor analysis of Nissl-stained histology slides can reveal glial cell orientation along axons (Schurr and Mezer, 2021), but the resulting fiber orientations are in 2D; also, dehydration during staining can lead to tissue deformation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The resulting fiber orientations from structure-tensor analysis of Nissl-stained histology slides are in 2D.
source: Structure-tensor analysis of Nissl-stained histology slides can reveal glial cell orientation along axons (Schurr and Mezer, 2021), but the resulting fiber orientations are in 2D; also, dehydration during staining can lead to tissue deformation.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the technique, representing established knowledge.

claim: Dehydration during histological staining can lead to tissue deformation.
source: Structure-tensor analysis of Nissl-stained histology slides can reveal glial cell orientation along axons (Schurr and Mezer, 2021), but the resulting fiber orientations are in 2D; also, dehydration during staining can lead to tissue deformation.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of histological staining, representing established knowledge.

claim: Serial electron microscopy enables the analysis of brain tissue structures at the highest detail.
source: Serial electron microscopy (Eberle and Zeidler, 2018; Salo et al., 2021) enables the analysis of brain tissue structures at the highest detail, but is only feasible for very small sample sizes and also requires a complex and specific sample preparation, preventing the reuse of samples for other purposes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about serial electron microscopy.

claim: Serial electron microscopy is only feasible for very small sample sizes.
source: Serial electron microscopy (Eberle and Zeidler, 2018; Salo et al., 2021) enables the analysis of brain tissue structures at the highest detail, but is only feasible for very small sample sizes and also requires a complex and specific sample preparation, preventing the reuse of samples for other purposes.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of serial electron microscopy, representing established knowledge.

claim: Serial electron microscopy requires a complex and specific sample preparation, preventing the reuse of samples for other purposes.
source: Serial electron microscopy (Eberle and Zeidler, 2018; Salo et al., 2021) enables the analysis of brain tissue structures at the highest detail, but is only feasible for very small sample sizes and also requires a complex and specific sample preparation, preventing the reuse of samples for other purposes.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of serial electron microscopy, representing established knowledge.

claim: Tissue clearing followed by labeling and fluorescence microscopy imaging has served as validation for dMRI data in recent years.
source: To assess microscopic fiber structures in 3D volumes (without sectioning), tissue clearing followed by labeling and fluorescence microscopy imaging is commonly used. In recent years, it has served as validation for dMRI data (Morawski et al., 2018; Stolp et al., 2018; Goubran et al., 2019; Leuze et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The tissue clearing process causes tissue deformation.
source: However, the clearing process causes tissue deformation (Leuze et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Optical coherence tomography relies on the back-scattering of light from a tissue block and images the superficial tissue layer before sectioning.
source: Other methods to study nerve fiber structures in 3D and microscopic detail (without clearing) are two-photon fluorescence microscopy (Zong et al., 2017; Costantini et al., 2021), or optical coherence tomography (Magnain et al., 2015; Men et al., 2016) which relies on the back-scattering of light from a tissue block and images the superficial tissue layer before sectioning.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and describes the principle of optical coherence tomography.

claim: All previously mentioned methods (histology, electron microscopy, clearing, OCT) require a directional analysis of the microscopic image data to extract orientation information.
source: All previously mentioned methods require a directional analysis of the microscopic image data to extract orientation information (structure tensor analysis – Khan et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about a common requirement of these methods, supported by citations.

claim: For structure tensor analysis, a kernel including several neighboring image pixels is used, which limits the resolution.
source: For this purpose, a kernel including several neighboring image pixels is used, which limits the resolution; also, in regions with densely packed nerve fibers, intensity gradients are low, limiting analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of structure tensor analysis, representing established knowledge.

claim: In regions with densely packed nerve fibers, intensity gradients are low, limiting structure tensor analysis.
source: For this purpose, a kernel including several neighboring image pixels is used, which limits the resolution; also, in regions with densely packed nerve fibers, intensity gradients are low, limiting analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of structure tensor analysis, representing established knowledge.

claim: Optical coherence tomography can be combined with polarized light (PS-OCT), which exploits the optical anisotropy (birefringence) of myelinated axons to determine their orientations.
source: To directly obtain the axonal orientations, optical coherence tomography can be combined with polarized light (PS-OCT), which exploits the optical anisotropy (birefringence) of myelinated axons to determine their orientations (Wang et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Polarization microscopy uses polarized light passed through thin brain sections and measures alterations in the polarization state.
source: A similar principle is used in polarization microscopy where polarized light is passed through thin brain sections and alterations in the polarization state are measured – a technique known for more than a century (Brodmann, 1903; Fraher and MacConaill, 1970).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and describes the principle of polarization microscopy.

claim: Three-dimensional polarized light imaging enabled the determination of 3D fiber orientations.
source: Recent advances realized polarization microscopy also in reflection mode (Takata et al., 2018), and three-dimensional polarized light imaging enabled the determination of 3D fiber orientations (Axer et al., 2011a; Axer et al., 2011b; Menzel et al., 2015; Zeineh et al., 2017; Stacho et al., 2020; Takemura et al., 2020) using an advanced signal analysis (Menzel et al., 2022) or a tiltable specimen stage (Schmitz et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In contrast to SLI, polarization microscopy techniques yield only a single fiber orientation for each measured tissue voxel.
source: However, in contrast to SLI, the techniques yield only a single fiber orientation for each measured tissue voxel, and voxels with multiple crossing fibers may yield erroneous fiber orientations (Dohmen et al., 2015), while retrieving the out-of-plane angle is also challenging.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents a known limitation of polarization microscopy.

claim: Voxels with multiple crossing fibers may yield erroneous fiber orientations in polarization microscopy.
